title: The Slope in the extraNonce: a Buenos Aires Cryptographer, the Bug Reports, and the Miner Who Never Spent
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Applied Cryptography, and the Networks of a Branch of the Government

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the book on cryptography
stops.date_confidence: self-reported and internally contradictory. Lerner's About page at bitslog.com dates his purchase of Bruce Schneier's Applied Cryptography to 1990, but that book's first edition was published in 1994. The recollection is his; the year cannot be right as stated, and no source reached resolves which end of the discrepancy is wrong. Month and day default to January. The pin is the Buenos Aires city centroid inherited byte-identical from cristina_fernandez_de_kirchner.journey.json and asserts no address. No reliable public source establishes his birth date or birthplace; a commercial biography site's figure of 1972 conflicts with the documented UBA record and is not corroborated anywhere.
stops.campa: A young man in Buenos Aires buys a copy of Bruce Schneier's Applied Cryptography and does not put it down. He will name that book, decades later, as the door he walked through: the place where the arithmetic of large primes became something a person could do to another person, or prevent. Nothing else of the household enters the public record. No birth notice, no school, no street. The whole of his childhood survives as one line on his own blog, naming a book, and giving it a year in which the book did not yet exist.
suggested_refs: Bruce Schneier, Applied Cryptography, first edition 1994, the book Lerner credits with his entry into the field

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the networks of a branch of the government
stops.date_confidence: self-reported, undated within the year. bitslog.com/about/ is the only source for this employment and it names no agency, no office and no month; January is set to order the segment. The pin is the Buenos Aires centroid and asserts no building.
stops.campa: By 1994 he is inside a government network, hardening Linux kernels, running intrusion detection, breaking ciphers in order to find out where they break. Which branch of the Argentine state is never said, not by him and not by anyone else; the sentence on his blog stops exactly where a name would go. This is the ordinary apprenticeship of the Buenos Aires security trade in the decade the country wired itself: young men learning attack in order to be paid for defense. The offices appear in no directory.
stops.quote: by 1994 I was working on information security... in order to protect the networks of a branch of Argentina's government
suggested_refs: bitslog.com/about/, the sole source for the government-network years and the only place the claim is made

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the cryptographic servers at Core Security
stops.date_confidence: the fact is self-attested and the date is not. bitslog.com/about/ records the Core Security consulting with no year, office or project named. Core Security Technologies was founded in Buenos Aires in 1996 by Emiliano Kargieman, Ivan Arce, Ariel Futoransky and Gerardo Richarte, per emiliano_kargieman.journey.json, and 1998 is set here only to place the stop after that founding. No source documents a personal meeting between Lerner and any named founder; the crossing is institutional, not attested as personal.
stops.campa: He consults for Core Security Technologies, the firm Emiliano Kargieman and Ivan Arce and Ariel Futoransky and Gerardo Richarte had built out of a flat in this city, and what he does there is design and code high-performance cryptographic servers. Argentina in these years exports two things to the security industry: exploits, and the people who write them. Twenty-seven years later Futoransky will put his name beside Lerner's on a paper about Bitcoin bridges. Whether the two men are ever in the same room in 1998, nobody recorded.
stops.quote: I worked as security consultant for Core Security... designing and programming high-performance cryptographic servers
suggested_refs: emiliano_kargieman.journey.json, stop 'Buenos Aires, six founders and a flat', for the 1996 founding of Core Security

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Pentatek and the neurological equipment
stops.date_confidence: self-reported and wholly undated. bitslog.com/about/ says he co-founded Pentatek and ATI-Medical and stayed with it more than ten years; no incorporation date, dissolution date, equity or co-founder beyond himself was located in any source reached. The year 2000 is an ordering device and nothing more, and the pin is the city centroid.
stops.campa: He co-founds Pentatek, later ATI-Medical, and for more than ten years builds machines that watch nervous systems: real-time signal processing, monitors for the surgeon's table, about fifteen people on the payroll. The cryptographer's decade and the medical-instrument decade run through the same man in the same city and neither appears in the other's paperwork. No incorporation record, no dissolution, no partner's name has been found. He is running a small factory through the years the country defaults on its debt.
stops.quote: a high-tech neurological equipment manufacturer in Latam, employing about 15 people, during more than 10 years
suggested_refs: Pentatek / ATI-Medical, unlocated in any Argentine corporate register reached for this file

segments.name: Mental Poker: Cards Nobody Can See

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the priority date of the shuffled deck
stops.date_confidence: attested. Google Patents records a priority date of 13 October 2009 for US8677128B2, filed 13 October 2010 and granted 18 March 2014, inventor Sergio Demian Lerner, assignee an individual. A related application, US8862879B2, carries its own priority of 13 April 2011 and does not belong to the 2009 family; the two are frequently folded together and should not be. No address appears on the filings reached and the pin is the city centroid.
stops.campa: The problem is old and elegant. Two players, no dealer, no trusted third party, and a deck that has to be shuffled so that neither can see it and neither can cheat. Cryptographers call it mental poker. On the thirteenth of October 2009 Lerner fixes a priority date over a family of commutative-cipher shuffling methods. The underlying question is how strangers who trust nothing can nonetheless agree on what happened. Bitcoin is nine months old that week. He has not heard of it, and the filing names no company, only him.
suggested_refs: US8677128B2, Method and apparatus for shuffling and dealing cards, priority 13 October 2009

stops.name: Ciudad Universitaria, Certimix enters the incubator
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact, approximate as to date and pin. incubacen.exactas.uba.ar records Certimix and its CertifiedPlay library in pre-incubation at Incubacen, the technology-business incubator of the Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales of the UBA. Incubacen sits in Pabellon II of Ciudad Universitaria; the coordinates given are the Nominatim resolution of Pabellon I, roughly a hundred and fifty metres away, and assert the pavilions rather than the office. Month unrecorded, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Certimix is a company built to sell a library, and the library does one thing: it lets people play cards across a network with no house. He calls the product CertifiedPlay. It enters pre-incubation at Incubacen, the business incubator that Exactas keeps in the raw concrete pavilions on the northern edge of the city, where biologists and mathematicians share corridors with whatever the students are trying to turn into a firm this year. The wind off the Plata comes through the open stairwells all winter.
suggested_refs: Incubacen, the Exactas-UBA technology incubator at Ciudad Universitaria, Pabellon II

stops.name: Ciudad Universitaria, the thesis on mental poker
stops.date_confidence: the thesis is real; the submission date is not confirmed. MPF: A New Family of Practical and Secure Mental Poker Protocols is indexed as Lerner's licenciatura thesis in computer science at Exactas, UBA, supervised by Hugo Scolnik, through academia.edu and dblp, and Scolnik's supervision is consistent with his own staff page at staff.dc.uba.ar/hscolnik/. The date of 15 November 2010 could not be verified against any reachable primary UBA record in this pass. The pin resolves Pabellon I, where the Departamento de Computacion sits.
stops.campa: He submits the thesis to the Departamento de Computacion under Hugo Scolnik, who has spent his own career on factoring and on the mathematics of Argentine cryptography. MPF is a family of protocols rather than a single scheme, and its point is practicality: mental poker had been solvable for thirty years and unusably slow for thirty years. The dedication is to his wife Alush and his son Ariel. That page is the only place in the whole reachable record of his life where a family appears at all.
suggested_refs: Sergio Demian Lerner, MPF: A New Family of Practical and Secure Mental Poker Protocols, licenciatura thesis, FCEN-UBA

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo, the third prize
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the prize, unverified as to the money and the room. The Incubacen post of 6 December 2010 confirms third place in the Idea-proyecto category of the second Concurso de Emprendimientos Innovadores run by Fundacion Empretec with the Banco de la Nacion Argentina. A widely repeated figure of ten thousand pesos could not be checked: empretec.org.ar and comercioyjusticia.info both returned HTTP 403 in this pass. The pin is the bank's Bartolome Mitre 326 headquarters, and no source places the ceremony inside it.
stops.campa: A cryptographic card-shuffling library takes third prize in the idea category of a competition run by the national bank and a foundation for entrepreneurs. It is the kind of award a country hands out when it wants innovation and has a small budget for wanting it. Whether the prize was ten thousand pesos, whether anyone stood up in the marble hall on Bartolome Mitre to collect it, the reachable record does not say. Certimix will be gone within four years, and the name will survive in one place: the byline on his Bitcoin vulnerability reports.
suggested_refs: Concurso de Emprendimientos Innovadores 2010, Fundacion Empretec and Banco de la Nacion Argentina, Idea-proyecto category

stops.name: Buenos Aires, reading the paper late in the year
stops.date_confidence: self-reported, month unrecorded, and contradicted by his own later account. bitslog.com/about/ dates his first reading of the Bitcoin paper to late 2011 and says he considered himself part of the community by the beginning of 2012; November is set to order the segment. The same page records him discussing anonymous payment systems on a cryptography mailing list in 2010 and says he does not remember reading about Bitcoin that year. A 2024 Criptonoticias interview instead dates his encounter to 2012. The discrepancy is his own and is left standing.
stops.campa: He reads the nine pages and goes straight to the source code, which is the reflex of a man who has been paid for fifteen years to find what is wrong with things. What he sees first is not the elegance. It is the attack surface: transactions that cost more to verify than to make, an alert system signed with a single key. The community that will later call him an early believer meets him first as a critic, writing to the developers privately, one flaw at a time. By the beginning of 2012, by his own reckoning, he is part of it.
stops.quote: It was not until late 2011, when I first read the Bitcoin paper and I rushed to analyze the source code
suggested_refs: The Bitcoin whitepaper of October 2008, read in Buenos Aires three years after publication

stops.name: Bitcoin Core 0.6.3, the exhausted processor
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Bitcoin Core 0.6.3 release notes of 25 June 2012 credit Sergio Lerner for responsible disclosure of a CPU-exhaustion denial-of-service flaw, catalogued afterward as CVE-2012-3789. The disclosure was made remotely and no source places him anywhere but at home, so the stop sits at his own Buenos Aires pin.
stops.campa: The bug is not glamorous. A crafted message makes every node on the network burn processor time for nothing, and a network of machines that will burn processor time for nothing can be stopped by one person with a laptop. He reports it privately and waits. The pattern will hold for eighteen months: find the way to make the whole thing sit down, tell four people, wait for the fix, then say so out loud. On the twenty-fifth of June the fix ships in 0.6.3 and the release notes name him. It is catalogued afterward as CVE-2012-3789.
suggested_refs: CVE-2012-3789, National Vulnerability Database

stops.name: Buenos Aires, MavePay at Ekoparty
stops.date_confidence: attested talk, contested venue. The Full Disclosure announcement at seclists.org/fulldisclosure/2012/Sep/30 gives the eighth Ekoparty, trainings 17 to 18 September and conference 19 to 21 September 2012, lists Bitcoin, MavePay and the Future of Cryptocurrencies on the program, and gives the location only as Ciudad Autonoma de Buenos Aires. Two secondary traditions place this same talk in two different buildings, the Aeroparque Jorge Newbery grounds and the Ciudad Cultural Konex, and neither is sourced to a primary document; the contradiction is left open and the pin defaults to the city centroid rather than choose. The frequent claim that 2012 was Ekoparty's tenth-anniversary edition is wrong: Spanish Wikipedia and the program itself both make it the eighth. The MAVEPAY paper PDF carries a creation date of 17 April 2012 and a single author.
stops.campa: He walks onto the Ekoparty stage billed as chief executive of Certimix, founder of Pentatek and independent security researcher, and hands the room a payment scheme of his own together with a list of ways to knock Bitcoin over. MAVEPAY is lighter than Bitcoin on purpose: a peer-to-peer currency protocol that does not require every participant to carry everything. The security conference that raised him is the first audience he brings any of this to. One tradition puts the stage at Aeroparque, another at the Konex.
suggested_refs: Sergio Demian Lerner, MAVEPAY, a new lightweight payment scheme for peer to peer currency networks, April 2012

stops.name: Bitcoin 0.7.0, the malleable alert
stops.date_confidence: attested. en.bitcoin.it/wiki/CVE-2012-4684 records Lerner's private report of a signature-malleability flaw in the alert system and his discussion of it with Gavin Andresen and Gregory Maxwell on 24 to 26 August 2012, the fix shipping in Bitcoin 0.7.0 on 17 September 2012 and public disclosure on 1 March 2013, after a large majority of reachable nodes had upgraded. Remote disclosure; the pin is his own.
stops.campa: Bitcoin carries an alert system, a channel by which the developers can shout at every node at once, and it is signed with one key. Lerner finds that the signature can be reshaped without being invalidated, which means an alert can be altered in flight. He writes to Gavin Andresen and Gregory Maxwell in the last days of August and the three of them sit on it. The fix goes out on the seventeenth of September. He waits until the first of March, until the count of upgraded nodes is high enough, and only then publishes.
suggested_refs: CVE-2012-4684, alert-system signature malleability, disclosed publicly 1 March 2013

stops.name: Bitcoin 0.8, the disk that seeks forever
stops.date_confidence: attested. en.bitcoin.it/wiki/CVE-2013-2293 records the report on 9 January 2013 by Sergio Demian Lerner of Certimix.com to Gavin Andresen and other core developers, Andresen's same-day confirmation that 0.8 would not be vulnerable, release candidate 1 on 9 February 2013 and public disclosure on 14 February 2013. Some accounts date the report to 8 January; the wiki gives the ninth. A source formerly cited for this episode, bitcoinwiki.org/wiki/cve-2013-2293, returns HTTP 404 and has been replaced.
stops.campa: This one does not exhaust the processor. It exhausts the disk. A transaction can be built that sends the node's read head hunting across the database, seek after seek, for as long as the attacker cares to keep paying almost nothing. He sends it to Andresen on the ninth of January and Andresen answers the same day that the coming 0.8, with its new database layer, will not be vulnerable. The release candidate ships on the ninth of February. He signs the report from Certimix, the card-game company.
suggested_refs: CVE-2013-2293, continuous disk seek denial of service, disclosed 14 February 2013

stops.name: Bitcoin, the transaction that takes three minutes
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the flaw and the date, unverified as to its publication. The CVE table at en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Common_Vulnerabilities_and_Exposures dates CVE-2013-2292 to 30 January 2013 and describes it as a transaction that takes at least three minutes to verify. A commonly cited NVD publication date of 12 March 2013 could not be confirmed: nvd.nist.gov and cve.org both failed to return the record in this pass, and en.bitcoin.it/wiki/CVE-2013-2292 returns HTTP 404.
stops.campa: Every signature check inside a Bitcoin transaction costs the network something, and nothing in the rules of 2013 stops one transaction from asking for a very great many of them. Lerner builds the transaction that takes three minutes to verify and shows what a mempool full of them would do to a chain whose blocks arrive every ten. Some of the press that follows him in this period prefers the headline about killing Bitcoin. The people fixing it prefer the number.
suggested_refs: CVE-2013-2292, OP_CHECKSIG validation cost, reported 30 January 2013
sources: nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2013-2292 (record not returned in this pass)

stops.name: Retiro, the office of Wences Casares
stops.date_confidence: the meeting is attested by Lerner himself and its date is not. bitslog.com/about/ records that in 2013 Wences Casares, founder of Xapo, visited Argentina, invited Lerner to his Buenos Aires offices, and convinced him to attend the Bitcoin conference in San Jose that May; March is set here only to place the stop before that conference. No source reached gives the office address and the pin is an approximation within the Retiro business district.
stops.campa: Wences Casares comes back to Argentina, as he does, and asks the cryptographer who has spent a year filing bug reports against Bitcoin to come and talk. The two share one obsession from opposite temperaments: Casares believes and has been telling anyone who will sit still since 2011, while Lerner audits. What they turn out to have in common is not conviction but curiosity about where the thing came from. Casares talks him into a ticket to California. Lerner has never seen the faces of the people whose code he has been breaking.
stops.quote: In 2013, Wences Casares, the founder of Xapo, visited Argentina... he invited me to his offices in Buenos Aires, and after a really enthusiastic talk he convinced me to go to the 2013 Bitcoin conference, in San Jose.
suggested_refs: wences_casares.journey.json, for the other side of this meeting

stops.name: Bitslog, the well deserved fortune
stops.date_confidence: attested; the post was fetched directly at bitslog.com/2013/04/17/the-well-deserved-fortune-of-satoshi-nakamoto/. Two things commonly attached to it belong elsewhere: the post does not use the word Patoshi, and it does not give the narrower figure of 1.1 million bitcoins. Both come from the 2019 work. What it says is that the estimate, at eyesight, is around one million.
stops.campa: Every mined block carries a small counter the miner increments while searching, the extraNonce, left in the coinbase transaction like a scratch in wet cement. Lerner plots them across the first fifty thousand blocks. What comes out is not noise. It is a set of straight line segments, one entity, restarting its counter at intervals, running a single machine on a deliberate schedule, and never once spending what it earned. He publishes on the seventeenth of April. Thirty-five thousand people read it inside a week.
stops.quote: I estimate at eyesight that Satoshi fortune is around 1M Bitcoins, or 100M USD at current exchange rate.
stops.quote_source: Sergio Demian Lerner, The Well Deserved Fortune of Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitslog, 17 April 2013
suggested_refs: Dominic Frisby, Bitcoin: The future of money? (Unbound, 2014), which reports this analysis to a general readership
sources: openlibrary.org full-text search, Dominic Frisby, Bitcoin: The future of money?, OL39827629M

stops.name: San Jose, the real faces
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the conference, self-reported as to what happened in it. Bitcoin 2013: The Future of Payments ran 17 to 19 May 2013 at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center. Lerner's account of attending, of pitching Appecoin and a Turing-complete contract platform, and of Timo Hanke being nearly the only interested listener is his own at bitslog.com/about/ and is not independently corroborated.
stops.campa: He flies to California and finds the community he had until then only argued with by mail, walking around a convention center: Andresen, Maxwell, the names from the release notes. He pitches two things. One is Appecoin. The other is a Turing-complete platform for contracts built on top of Bitcoin, eighteen months before the Ethereum white paper. Almost nobody wants to hear it. One German mathematician does. His name is Timo Hanke, and nobody else who was in that hall has ever written the scene down.
suggested_refs: Bitcoin 2013: The Future of Payments, San Jose McEnery Convention Center, 17 to 19 May 2013

stops.name: Ciudad Cultural Konex, the mystery trip
stops.date_confidence: the talk is attested; the venue and month are not. Lerner's own talk list gives Satoshi Nakamoto, in Spanish, 2013, EkoParty Conference, and a recording circulates under the title A Mystery Trip to the Origin of Bitcoin. Ciudad Cultural Konex at Sarmiento 3131 is Ekoparty's customary Buenos Aires home in these years but has not been pinned to the 2013 edition by any primary program reached; the coordinates are the Nominatim resolution of Konex. September is the conference's usual month and is set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Five months after the blog post he takes the research to a stage in Buenos Aires and gives it in Spanish, to a room of Argentine security people who have known him since before Bitcoin existed. The talk is a detective story and he tells it as one: here is the fingerprint, here is what it cannot prove, here is the man who left it and never came back for the money. Someone puts a camera on it. The recording circulates under a title he did not give it, A Mystery Trip to the Origin of Bitcoin.
suggested_refs: YouTube recording, Sergio Demian Lerner, A mystery trip to the origin of Bitcoin, Ekoparty 2013

stops.name: Melia Buenos Aires, the first LaBitConf
stops.date_confidence: the conference is attested; Lerner's presence in the hall is not. blog.portinos.com confirms verbatim that the first Latin American Bitcoin conference ran on 7 and 8 December 2013 at the Melia Buenos Aires Hotel, Reconquista 945, and names Jeff Garzik and Tony Gallippi as the headline foreign speakers. Names widely repeated elsewhere for this edition, Andreas Antonopoulos and Erik Voorhees, could not be verified in this pass and are not asserted here. No primary source places Lerner at this specific edition; he is documented as belonging to the Buenos Aires circle that the conference gathered, not as a speaker at it.
stops.campa: The first Latin American Bitcoin conference is held in a hotel on Reconquista, two blocks off the old financial district, and it collects into one building a scene that had until then been meeting in bars: Diego Gutierrez Zaldivar, who organized it, Wences Casares, who had been evangelizing since 2011, the Fundacion Bitcoin Argentina people, the developers. Lerner belongs to that circle by every account of it. Whether he walked into the Melia on the seventh of December, no document reached here says.
suggested_refs: wences_casares.journey.json
The forthcoming journey file for Diego Gutierrez Zaldivar, organizer of the first LaBitConf
sources: blog.portinos.com, 'Buenos Aires, sede del primer encuentro Bitcoin de Latinoamerica'
bitcoinmagazine.com, 'First Latin American Bitcoin Conference Set to Take Place in Argentina'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the collaboration with Timo Hanke
stops.date_confidence: attested with a dating conflict left unresolved. Lerner says the collaboration ran during 2014. The patent record puts the priority earlier: US11113676B2, Block mining methods and apparatus, inventors Timo Tobias Hanke and Sergio Demian Lerner, carries a priority date of 19 November 2013, was filed 28 April 2016, granted 7 September 2021, and is assigned to Circle Line International Limited. January 2014 orders the segment and does not adjudicate. A claim in circulation that the patent gives Lerner a Buenos Aires residence does not appear on the Google Patents record reached, and patents.justia.com returned HTTP 403.
stops.campa: The optimization is arithmetic, not engineering. SHA-256 hashes the block header twice, and a miner who chooses his candidate headers carefully can reuse part of the first pass across many attempts instead of redoing it each time. Hanke and Lerner work it out and file on it. The saving is something like a fifth of the electricity, which in an industry that is nothing but electricity is an enormous quantity of money. Three years later, covert use of the same trick by mining manufacturers becomes a central charge in the scaling war.
stops.quote: During 2014 I collaborated with Timo Hanke in creating ASICBoost... which became a novelistic story that had a happy end
suggested_refs: US11113676B2, Block mining methods and apparatus, granted 7 September 2021
Malicious Life podcast, episode on ASICBoost, for the SegWit-era controversy the technique was drawn into

stops.name: CoinFabrik, Buenos Aires
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the founding and the partners, unattested as to the year. bitslog.com/about/ names Pablo Yabo and Sebastian Wain as co-founders and gives the figure of more than forty engineers, with no date attached. The commonly repeated circa-2014 dating rests on corporate profiles rather than on any record reached here; June 2014 is set only to order the segment.
stops.campa: With Pablo Yabo and Sebastian Wain he builds a software factory for cryptocurrency work, and it grows past forty engineers, which in the Buenos Aires of these years makes it one of the largest single concentrations of blockchain developers anywhere south of the equator. The country's chronic export is programmer-hours priced in a currency that keeps losing. CoinFabrik sells them by the month to companies in San Francisco and Berlin, and the engineers stay in Palermo and are paid in dollars.
stops.quote: I co-founded Coinfabrik with Pablo Yabo and Sebastian Wain. Coinfabrik used to employ more than 40 engineers
suggested_refs: CoinFabrik, Buenos Aires, co-founded with Pablo Yabo and Sebastian Wain

stops.name: The Bitcoin Foundation, the auditor on demand
stops.date_confidence: attested, with a date to keep straight. The Bitcoin Foundation announcement by chief scientist Gavin Andresen is dated 5 December 2014 per CoinDesk; the Spanish-language reprint at oroyfinanzas.com that carries the quoted passage is dated 8 December, and the two are frequently conflated. Some outlets described the role as full time; Andresen's own text and Lerner's clarification both make it on demand. The appointment was remote, so the stop sits at his own pin, and the oroyfinanzas article confirms he kept consulting for Coinspect from Buenos Aires while holding it.
stops.campa: The Foundation hires him to read the code, which he has been doing for free since March 2012. He is now paid, occasionally, by the institution whose software he had spent two years demonstrating he could stop. Andresen's announcement is careful about the shape of the thing: not a salaried developer but an auditor called when there is something to audit, because the people who keep Bitcoin alive have jobs and families and hobbies outside it. Part of the press reports a full-time hire anyway, and Lerner corrects them.
stops.quote: La gente está ocupada. Tienen vidas, familias, carreras y pasatiempos fuera del Bitcoin. No es realista poner las expectativas de un empleado a tiempo completo en un voluntario.
stops.quote_source: Gavin Andresen, Bitcoin Foundation announcement, in the Spanish translation published by Oro y Finanzas, December 2014
suggested_refs: Gavin Andresen's Bitcoin Foundation announcement of 5 December 2014
sources: coindesk.com, 'Bitcoin Foundation Hires Developer Sergio Lerner for Full-Time Security Role' (5 December 2014)
oroyfinanzas.com, 'Sergio Lerner contratado como auditor de seguridad de Bitcoin' (8 December 2014)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Coinspect with Juliano Rizzo
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the partnership, unattested as to the year. bitslog.com/about/ names Juliano Rizzo as his co-founder at Coinspect, the cryptocurrency security-audit firm. No source reached gives a founding date; January 2015 is set only to order the stop before the July report that both men sign.
stops.campa: Coinspect audits other people's cryptocurrency code for money, and he starts it with Juliano Rizzo, who is known across the security world for BEAST and the padding-oracle work and belongs to the same Buenos Aires generation. The two firms divide his professional life cleanly. CoinFabrik builds; Coinspect breaks. The same division ran through his twenties, when he wrote cryptographic servers for one employer and hunted intruders for another. Rizzo will sign the Vot.Ar report beside him in July.
suggested_refs: Coinspect, Buenos Aires, co-founded with Juliano Rizzo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the signature on the Vot.Ar report
stops.date_confidence: attested, with two corrections to the usual account. The report on the multi-vote attack against the Vot.Ar electronic voting system is headed Julio 3, 2015 and was released through Fundacion Via Libre two days before the Buenos Aires city election of 5 July 2015, so that polling officers and scrutineers would be alert during the count. Lerner's name appears on its closing page under the heading Adhieren, which makes him a signatory rather than a listed co-author, alongside Alfredo Ortega, Ivan Ariel Barrera Oro, Enrique Chaparro, Fernando Russ, Francisco Amato, Javier Smaldone, Juliano Rizzo and Nicolas Waisman. It was not presented at Ekoparty, which ran in October that year. Pin is the city centroid; the report was published online.
stops.campa: Buenos Aires is about to vote on machines, and a group of Argentine security researchers publishes what the machines will let a person do: cast more than one vote from a single ballot card. The document goes out on the third of July, two days before the election, timed so that the people counting will know what to watch for. Lerner's name sits on the last page under the word Adhieren, with Rizzo and Smaldone and Ortega and the rest, above a line that reads: and people of the Internet.
suggested_refs: Ataque Multi-Voto a Sistema Vot.Ar, Fundacion Via Libre, 3 July 2015

segments.name: Rootstock: a Second Chain Under the Same Hammer

stops.name: Buenos Aires, RSK Labs founded
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year and the founders, approximate as to the month. Lerner, Diego Gutierrez Zaldivar, Adrian Eidelman, Gabriel Kurman and Ruben Altman founded RSK Labs in Buenos Aires in 2015. Crunchbase dates Gutierrez Zaldivar's tenure as chief executive from November 2015, which is the basis for the month set here. No office address is attested in any source reached and the pin is the city centroid.
stops.campa: Five people start a company to do the thing Bitcoin was designed not to do. RSK is a sidechain: a second blockchain merge-mined by the same hardware that mines Bitcoin, carrying an Ethereum-compatible virtual machine and a bridge that moves coins across and back. Lerner designs the merge-mining, designs the bridge, writes the whitepaper. Diego Gutierrez Zaldivar, who two years earlier had filled a hotel on Reconquista, runs the company. The name changes twice, Rootstock to RSK to Rootstock, and the oldest one keeps returning.
stops.quote: In 2015 I co-founded RSK Labs and we raised money to develop the first Bitcoin sidechain... I designed Rootstock, including its merge-mining subsystem and its bridge with Bitcoin, and I wrote its whitepaper

stops.name: Bitslog, the revenge of Patoshi
stops.date_confidence: attested; the post was fetched directly at bitslog.com/2019/04/16/the-return-of-the-deniers-and-the-revenge-of-patoshi/. The nickname Patoshi and the narrower coin figures belong to this phase of the work, not to the 2013 post. The critical position against him, that a restricted nonce range and a slope pattern establish one implementation rather than one identifiable person, is a synthesized analyst consensus rather than a single dated statement, and is rendered here as a live dispute.

He looks instead at the least significant byte of each winning nonce and finds it confined to a narrow range in precisely the blocks the older method had flagged, which is a second fingerprint left by the same hand and independent of the first. Then he adds the timestamps. No inversions at all, across forty-three percent of the first fifty thousand blocks. What his critics still answer is that one machine is not the same claim as one man.

stops.name: RSK, the Powpeg

The naming of his co-designers is not given on that page and none was located elsewhere in this pass.
stops.campa: The oldest objection to sidechains is the peg. Whoever holds the coins on the Bitcoin side can take them, and a federation of signers is a federation of people who can be leaned on. The Powpeg answers it with hardware: the signing keys live inside purpose-built modules that will only sign what the proof of work says is true, and the humans running the boxes cannot reach inside. It does not abolish trust. It moves trust out of a list of names and into a piece of silicon, and it says so openly. Who else designed it with him, he does not say.

stops.name: Fairgate, auditable proof of work
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, weakly sourced, and the weakest item in this file. APoW: Auditable Proof-of-Work Against Block Withholding Attacks appears in the works bibliography of the research dossier compiled for this journey and is consistent with Fairgate's active programme on BitVMX, garbled circuits and covenants, but no primary record of its publication was reached in this pass and no month is attested. The proposal makes the work auditable, so that not handing it in leaves a trace. Nobody has established the year he was born.
